A little help with your daily practice.
Some days it is easy to settle into japa. On other days, your mind wanders. That is part of practice. There is no need to judge the session or look for a special experience.
The main Gayatri verse has 24 syllables, called aksharas. Listen to how each one sounds, then give it enough time as you recite. You can replay the recording whenever you need a reminder.
Listen for the rise and fall
In Vedic chanting, the pitch rises and falls in a pattern called swara. Listen to a short part of the recording and try it slowly. A teacher can help you learn the details.
A pause at three times of day
Sandhya Vandan brings prayer into the morning, midday, and evening. The app uses the sun times in your chosen location to help you remember. Start with a routine you can return to.
A mala has 108 beads to help you keep count as you recite. In the app, each accepted recitation adds to your total. Take your time with the words; the count can wait.

With time, you may find yourself remembering the mantra during an ordinary day. The tradition also describes ajapa, where japa continues without deliberate effort. It is not something you need to force.
Make it easy to come back
A familiar place and a regular time can make practice easier. Leave yourself a few unhurried minutes. If you miss a day, you can begin again when you are ready.
Shraddha means faith and sincerity. You do not have to rush to reach a number. A few recitations with care can be a good practice for today.

A longer commitment to Gayatri japa. Learn what it involves.

Purashcharana is a long-term commitment to recite a mantra 1,00,000 times for each syllable. The Gayatri verse has 24 syllables, so its full count is 24,00,000 recitations. This can take years. The app keeps your count and marks milestones along the way.
The 24 syllables belong to the main Gayatri verse. Om and the opening words Bhur, Bhuvah, and Svah are not included in this calculation.

This sets a goal of 24,00,000 Gayatri recitations, with no time limit. Your recorded Gayatri japa counts towards this goal. Pronunciation practice is kept separate. You can set the commitment aside at any time and keep your recorded progress.

Choose a regular time and a comfortable place where you can recite without rushing. A manageable daily count is easier to keep. Follow the guidance of your teacher or tradition as you settle into the practice.

Record your Gayatri japa after each Sandhya, or use the counter as you practise. Each repetition counts once towards the goals you had at that time. You can correct a saved count whenever you need to. When you are signed in, saved japa is backed up when this phone connects to the internet.
